newsitem.title: INDIA: Private sector key to funding Asia projects - HSBC.
newsitem.headline: Private sector key to funding Asia projects - HSBC.

text.p: Asia's huge infrastructure needs will be increasingly funded by private sector sources, said John Bond, group chief executive of HSBC Holdings Plc.
"Government cannot fund all projects, so it needs to tap all sources and be imaginative. This releases government money for other urgent needs," Bond told a group of industrialists.
The World Bank estimates Asia's infrastructure requirements at around $850 billion in the next five years of which India is expected to account for around $200 billion.
Bond said in countries like India public expenditure must take the lead especially for the development of ports and roads.

"The Indian government should participate with the private sector in bearing some of the various risks like interest rate risk, exchange rate risk and credit risk that go into an infrastructure project," he said.
"Private sector operators will be too expensive if they have to assume all the risks involved."
He said the establishment of a regulatory authority for each sector may also provide comfort to private investment.

Project finance where lending is repaid by cash flow from the project -- rather than lending based on physical value of assets or credit strength -- was the preferred form of private investment, Bond said.
"For projects to succeed, the basic risks must be right, the legal and documentary problems overcome and the macro-economic background constant," Bond said.
"It is no good moving the goalposts by, for instance, capping the rates of return as happened in China with some power projects."

He said project finance frees up government money reducing budget deficits and allows longer-term funding. Disadvantages include higher borrowing costs, more complex deals, greater syndication risk, higher monitoring requirements, and sometimes inflexible terms and conditions.
The HSBC group has been involved in financing several infrastructure projects in Asia including a $2.0 billion power station in the Guangdong province in China.
He said a key factor in the financing of the project was that a proportion of power sales was in foreign exchange.
"The power buyers performance of this obligation was guaranteed by the Guangdong International Trust and Investment Corporation," Bond said.

"Throughout Asia obtaining this kind of guarantee is probably the single most difficult obstacle to overcome, as it requires obtaining the support of institutions with credible access to foreign exchange."
